newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Bosnian Serb gets 20 years for war crimes.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb gets 20 years for war crimes.

text.p: The U.N. war crimes tribunal sentenced Bosnian Serb Dusan Tadic to 20 years in prison on Monday for taking part in a brutal "ethnic cleansing" campaign against Moslem civilians.

Tadic had been convicted on May 7 of war crimes and crimes against humanity in connection with atrocities including multiple beatings and two murders of Moslems in the early stages of Bosnia's 1992-95 war.

"You committed these crimes with intention and with sadistic brutality ... To condone your actions is to give effect to a base view of morality and invite anarchy," presiding judge Gabrielle Kirk McDonald told the court.
Tadic, 41, stood to hear the sentences read, looking pale and swallowing nervously. As he was led out of the chamber, he waved briefly to supporters in the public gallery.

During seven months of hearings last year, prosecutors charged that Tadic had rounded up his former Moslem neighbours in the Prijedor region of northwest Bosnia and tortured, raped and killed them in Serb-run detention camps.
A three-judge panel found him guilty on 11 counts of persecution and beatings, but not guilty on nine counts of murder, and they declared 11 charges inapplicable.
He was also found guilty of complicity in the killing of two policemen.

Tadic has always denied the charges, claiming he was a victim of the Moslems' desire to find a scapegoat for their suffering at the hands of the Serbs. His lawyers have lodged an appeal against the guilty verdict.
Tadic, who has already spent three years in custody, faced a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, the term demanded by the tribunal's prosecutors. The court could not impose a death penalty.
The International Tribunal on former Yugoslavia (ICTY), based in The Hague, has publicly indicted 76 suspects -- most of them Serbs -- but holds just 10 in its custody.
Its two "Most Wanted" men -- the wartime Bosnian Serb president, Radovan Karadzic, and former military commander, General Ratko Mladic, remain at large.
Monday's sentencing was the ICTY's first after a full-length trial.

The Prijedor purge was one of the worst crimes against civilians in the war. Non-Serbs, mostly Moslems but also Croats, were herded into three notorious prison camps -- Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje -- to be beaten, kept in inhumane conditions and, in some cases, executed.

This was part of what Western monitors and war-crimes prosecutors said was a systematic Serb policy of consolidating control over territory seized in war by detaining and then expelling and killing its non-Serb population.
Sentencing on Tadic coincided with a new toughening of efforts by NATO-led peacekeeping troops in Bosnia to apprehend fugitive indicted war criminals.
Last week, crack British troops in Prijedor shot dead regional police chief Simo Drljaca after he resisted capture and arrested hospital director Milan Kovacevic.
Both were the subject of secret tribunal indictments in connection with the 1992 events in Prijedor. Kovacevic is now jailed in The Hague awaiting trial.

U.N. war crimes tribunals for former Yugoslavia and Rwanda mark the first attempt to try war criminals before an international panel of judges since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials after World War Two.
